analysis.one_liner: Bans meatpackers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock before slaughter.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Agriculture Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend a 1921 law that was written to stop meatpacking companies from controlling the animals they slaughter. It would make it illegal for a packer to own, feed, or take operational control of livestock in a way that leaves the farmer raising it without real say over the operation. Farmers would keep ownership and management of their animals until close to slaughter, instead of raising them under contract for a packer's account.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and hog farmers, who would no longer compete against herds and flocks owned outright by the companies that buy their animals, and would keep more bargaining power over price. Shoppers could benefit indirectly if more independent sellers meant more competition in meat markets.

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit packers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock to the point that the producer no longer materially participates in managing the operation, so the farmer stays in charge of raising the animal.

The ban covers arrangements that give the packer operational, managerial, or supervisory control, whether held directly or through a subsidiary, closing the main routes by which packers integrate backward into raising livestock.
Existing arrangements would have a transition period: hog packers would have 18 months after enactment, and other livestock packers up to 180 days, to unwind arrangements that violate the ban.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would have to give up ownership and control of livestock feeding operations and buy animals on the open market instead; some of that cost could show up in meat prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains significant carve-outs: livestock held within 7 days of slaughter is exempt, cooperatives owned by active members are exempt, small packers that do not report daily price data are exempt, and any packer that owns only one processing plant is exempt, which narrows who is actually covered.

Packers argue that owning and feeding their own animals lets them control quality and stabilize supply, and that forcing divestiture could raise their costs, which could eventually reach consumers in meat prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would directly strengthen the bargaining position of independent farmers against a handful of very large meatpackers, which is its clear purpose. Its main weaknesses are the exemptions — a packer with a single plant is exempt, which spares some large processors — and the possibility of modest cost increases passed to consumers. On balance the benefits run to farmers and market competition, with the cost concentrated on the packing industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Grassley introduced the bill on May 10, 2016, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No committee action, hearing, floor vote, or further consideration ever followed, and the bill expired with the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's life.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies that own or control livestock before slaughter are better off, because the ban that would have forced them to divest those operations never advanced. Farmers who raise livestock under packer control gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban packer ownership of livestock and referred it to the Agriculture Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Large meatpacking industry
against.role: Beef and pork processors that own, feed, or contract livestock before slaughter
against.what_they_did: The bill would directly cost packers their livestock ownership and feeding arrangements; the industry has historically opposed packer ownership bans, and the committee never advanced the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so there is no record showing how the parties would have lined up; the sponsor was a Republican from a farm state.

industries.note: The bill would bar packers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock before slaughter, forcing companies like the major beef and pork processors to buy animals on the open market rather than raise them under their own control. It also allows existing arrangements to continue for up to 18 months for hog packers, softening the immediate hit.

industries.industry: Independent livestock producers (ranchers and hog farmers)
industries.note: Farmers would keep ownership and management of the animals they raise instead of competing against packer-owned herds, which strengthens their bargaining power on price.
Cooperatives majority-owned by active members who supply their own livestock for slaughter are exempt from the ban, preserving their ability to market members' animals while packers are restricted.
Packers that own only one processing plant, or that are not required to report daily price and quantity data, are exempt from the ban, so the rule falls only on larger multi-plant packers.
